verses.text: Then all the captains of the forces, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least even to the greatest, came near,

and said to Jeremiah the prophet, “Please let our supplication be presented before you, and pray for us to Yahweh your God, even for all this remnant; for we are left but a few of many, as your eyes do see us;
that Yahweh your God may show us the way in which we should walk, and the thing that we should do.”

Then Jeremiah the prophet said to them, “I have heard you; behold, I will pray to Yahweh your God according to your words; and it shall happen that whatever thing Yahweh shall answer you, I will declare it to you; I will keep nothing back from you.”
Then they said to Jeremiah, “May Yahweh be a true and faithful witness among us, if we don’t do according to all the word with which Yahweh your God shall send you to us.
Whether it is good, or whether it is bad, we will obey the voice of Yahweh our God, to whom we send you; that it may be well with us, when we obey the voice of Yahweh our God.”
After ten days, Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah.
Then he called Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces who were with him, and all the people from the least even to the greatest,
and said to them, “Yahweh, the God of Israel, to whom you sent me to present your supplication before him, says:
‘If you will still live in this land, then I will build you, and not pull you down, and I will plant you, and not pluck you up; for I grieve over the distress that I have brought on you.
Don’t be afraid of the king of Babylon, of whom you are afraid. Don’t be afraid of him,’ says Yahweh: ‘for I am with you to save you, and to deliver you from his hand.
I will grant you mercy, that he may have mercy on you, and cause you to return to your own land.
“‘But if you say, “We will not dwell in this land;” so that you don’t obey Yahweh your God’s voice,
saying, “No; but we will go into the land of Egypt, where we shall see no war, nor hear the sound of the trumpet, nor have hunger of bread; and there will we dwell:”’
now therefore hear Yahweh’s word, O remnant of Judah: Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says, ‘If you indeed set your faces to enter into Egypt, and go to live there;

then it shall happen, that the sword, which you fear, shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt; and the famine, about which you are afraid, shall follow close behind you there in Egypt; and you shall die there.

So shall it be with all the men who set their faces to go into Egypt to live there: they shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence; and none of them shall remain or escape from the evil that I will bring on them.’

For Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘As my anger and my wrath has been poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so shall my wrath be poured out on you, when you shall enter into Egypt; and you shall be an object of horror, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach; and you shall see this place no more.’
“Yahweh has spoken concerning you, remnant of Judah, Don’t you go into Egypt: know certainly that I have testified to you today.

For you have dealt deceitfully against your own souls; for you sent me to Yahweh your God, saying, ‘Pray for us to Yahweh our God; and according to all that Yahweh our God shall say, so declare to us, and we will do it:’
and I have declared it to you today; but you have not obeyed Yahweh your God’s voice in anything for which he has sent me to you.
Now therefore know certainly that you shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence, in the place where you desire to go to live there.”

footnotes.content: The captains and people gather—broken, surviving, stripped of everything but hope. Notice they come together, the whole remnant, from greatest to least. There's something holy in how the desperate learn to approach God through His prophet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They ask for intercession, not for comfort but for direction. 'We are left but a few'—they've counted their losses and know they cannot survive by their own wisdom. The humble asking opens the door; pride keeps it closed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The remnant doesn't ask *what they want to hear*; they ask for the way they should walk. Humility asks the right question. How many of us still struggle to seek God's will before our own path?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah promises faithfulness—he will hide nothing back. This is what a true prophet does: brings God's whole word, not the comfortable parts. 'I will keep nothing back' echoes the prophet's covenant to speak truth without fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They swear an oath before Yahweh—binding their own souls. 'May Yahweh be a true and faithful witness among us.' They're not swearing lightly; they're putting their whole future in God's hands as a pledge of obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They promise obedience before they hear the answer. 'Whether it is good, or whether it is bad, we will obey.' That's the hardest promise to keep—not when the path looks pleasant, but when it cuts against our desire.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten days of waiting. In that silence, faith is tested—no immediate word, no rush. God takes His time, and those who truly seek must learn to wait without wavering. The answer comes, but only after the testing of true surrender.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah gathers them all again—captains and people, great and small. The prophet includes the whole remnant in the hearing. God speaks to His people as a people, not to leaders alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophet speaks God's word directly—'Yahweh, the God of Israel...says.' No embellishment, no mediation through human interpretation. Just the word, delivered faithfully through the one commissioned to carry it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God offers tenderness: 'I will build you, not pull you down.' After all the judgment, He grieves over the distress He brought. Listen—even God's judgment is mingled with compassion for those who belong to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Don't be afraid of the king of Babylon, of whom you are afraid.' Fear names itself—twice. But God's promise is simple: 'I am with you to save you.' No charm or power compares to this presence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mercy leads to mercy—God will grant them compassion so that the king himself shows them mercy. Divine kindness often works through human hearts, when we remain where God has planted us and trust His method, not our escape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The turning point: 'If you say, We will not dwell in this land.' Notice how quickly refusal follows the promise. The human heart is quick to break its oath when fear whispers another way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They dream of Egypt—no war, no trumpet, no hunger. How seductive the false refuge sounds. We too are tempted by the promise that escape, not obedience, will save us. Egypt always looks safer than faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God calls them by their name: 'O remnant of Judah.' Even in the word of warning, He remembers them. The Lord of Armies does not speak to the faceless; He speaks to His own, those who bear His covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sword they flee will find them there; the famine they escape will follow. Running from God's will doesn't lead to safety—it only trades one danger for worse. The path not taken is the path that destroys.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All who choose Egypt will die by sword, famine, pestilence—'none of them shall remain or escape.' This is the hard mercy of truth: the prophet speaks the consequence so that hearts might turn. Love sometimes means speaking what is hard to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's wrath and sorrow are poured out alike—as they were on Jerusalem, so on those who flee Him. The objects of horror, astonishment, curse, and reproach—this is what disobedience looks like when stamped with God's judgment. The place is abandoned forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Don't you go into Egypt.' This is God's final word, spoken with certainty. He has testified to them—openly, clearly, without ambiguity. The remnant now knows the will of the Lord. What they do next is on their shoulders, not His.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophet names the deception they practice against themselves—they asked for God's word, swore to obey it, and already their hearts are prepared to break that oath. We deceive ourselves most deeply in the very act of making promises.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah has done his part faithfully. 'I have declared it to you today; but you have not obeyed.' The responsibility now falls where it always falls—on the hearer. God speaks; we choose. That choice shapes everything that follows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this warning: we too are tempted to run toward false security rather than trust God's hard word. The remnant's choice to flee to Egypt points to our own tendency to seek comfort over obedience, escape over faith. The God who spoke then still calls us to stay where He has placed us and trust His keeping.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
